Harness Engineering · Product Case Study #3 · Snapshot: September 2026 🐋

DeepSeek Harness (dsh): an Open-Source, Plugin-Composed Agent Runtime

The first two product case studies were managed harnesses you rent. DeepSeek Harness is the opposite bet: an MIT-licensed harness you own, where the model adapter, tools, sessions, sandboxes, storage, the agent loop and even the UI are all swappable plugins on the Cordis framework, and every model-visible fact is written to an append-only session log. This visual deep dive takes it apart from its repository and documentation — with interactive diagrams and a runnable miniature of its two core ideas.

How to read this: the third product case study (after OpenAI Agents API and Claude Agent SDK & Managed Agents). Facts come from the deepseek-harness repository, its architecture document and launch coverage, checked in September 2026 (see References). dsh is a developer preview — its own README warns that there will be compatibility-breaking changes. Diagrams simplify; the Python miniature is a teaching model, not dsh's TypeScript code.

01 What Is DeepSeek Harness (dsh)?

DeepSeek Harness, dsh for short, is an open-source agent harness from DeepSeek AI: the software between a language model and the outside world that supplies tools, sessions, sandboxing and the loop that keeps a task moving. DeepSeek released v0.1 as a developer preview on 13 August 2026 under the MIT licence, built on Node.js/TypeScript. Its one core idea: everything is a plugin.

05 Cordis: "Everything Is a Plugin"

Cordis is the plugin framework beneath dsh: plugins contribute services, typed events and reversible effects to a shared context. It grew out of the Koishi chatbot framework, built by the developer known as Shigma (Yifan Shi), and describes itself as a "meta-framework of spatiotemporal composability" — formalized with DeepSeek and Peking University researchers in A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability (arXiv:2608.25512). Two properties make hot-swapping safe:

Temporal composability
Every effect a plugin registers — a service, a listener, a timer — comes with a disposer. Unloading a plugin runs its disposers in reverse order, fully reverting its effects.
Spatial composability
Plugins declare which services they depend on; when a dependency appears, disappears or is replaced, dependents are reactively reloaded.
▶ Load, unload and hot-swap plugins Click plugins to toggle them. Watch the context, and the dispose order.

A runnable miniature of both core ideas — reversible plugin effects and an event-sourced session:

"""A miniature of the two ideas at the heart of DeepSeek Harness (dsh), in plain Python.

1. Cordis-style plugins: every effect a plugin registers (a service, an event listener, a tool)
   comes with a disposer; unloading the plugin runs its disposers in reverse order, so the
   system returns exactly to its previous state. That is what makes hot-swapping safe.
2. An event-sourced session log: an append-only list of events is the source of truth; the
   messages sent to the model are *derived* from it, so a turn can be replayed or forked.
This is a teaching model, not dsh's TypeScript code. Standard library only.
"""
class Context:
    def __init__(self):
        self.services, self.listeners, self.tools = {}, {}, {}

    def load(self, plugin):
        disposers = []
        def effect(do, undo):                     # every change carries its inverse
            do(); disposers.append(undo)
        plugin(self, effect)
        return lambda: [undo() for undo in reversed(disposers)]   # unload = revert in reverse

    def state(self):
        return f"services={sorted(self.services)} tools={sorted(self.tools)} listeners={sorted(self.listeners)}"

def deepseek_adapter(ctx, effect):
    effect(lambda: ctx.services.__setitem__("llm", "deepseek-v4.1-flash"), lambda: ctx.services.pop("llm"))

def openai_adapter(ctx, effect):
    effect(lambda: ctx.services.__setitem__("llm", "gpt-6-astra"), lambda: ctx.services.pop("llm"))

def shell_tools(ctx, effect):
    effect(lambda: ctx.tools.__setitem__("shell", "run commands"), lambda: ctx.tools.pop("shell"))
    effect(lambda: ctx.listeners.__setitem__("tool/call", "audit"), lambda: ctx.listeners.pop("tool/call"))

ctx = Context()
print("start:            ", ctx.state())
unload_model = ctx.load(deepseek_adapter)
unload_shell = ctx.load(shell_tools)
print("after loading:    ", ctx.state(), "->", ctx.services["llm"])
unload_model(); ctx.load(openai_adapter)          # hot-swap the model adapter
print("model swapped:    ", ctx.state(), "->", ctx.services["llm"])
unload_shell()
print("shell unloaded:   ", ctx.state())

# ── event-sourced session ──
log = [
    {"type": "turn/start", "turn": 1},
    {"type": "user/message", "text": "Investigate the failing service"},
    {"type": "step/start", "step": 1},
    {"type": "assistant/message", "text": "Checking pods.", "tool_call": "shell: kubectl get pods"},
    {"type": "tool/result", "tool": "shell", "status": "ok", "output": "api-7f 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff"},
    {"type": "step/end", "step": 1},
    {"type": "assistant/message", "text": "The api pod is crash-looping; reading its logs next."},
    {"type": "turn/end", "turn": 1},
]

def project(events):
    """Derive the model-visible messages from the log (the log is the only source of truth)."""
    msgs = []
    for e in events:
        if e["type"] == "user/message": msgs.append(("user", e["text"]))
        elif e["type"] == "assistant/message": msgs.append(("assistant", e["text"] + (f" [{e['tool_call']}]" if "tool_call" in e else "")))
        elif e["type"] == "tool/result": msgs.append(("tool", e["output"]))
    return msgs

print(f"\nsession log: {len(log)} events -> {len(project(log))} model-visible messages")
for role, text in project(log): print(f"   {role:<10} {text}")
fork = log[:5] + [{"type": "user/message", "text": "Actually, check the database first"}]
print(f"\nfork at event 5: {len(fork)} events; last derived message -> {project(fork)[-1]}")
print("replaying the same log always yields the same messages:", project(log) == project(list(log)))

Output:

start:             services=[] tools=[] listeners=[]
after loading:     services=['llm'] tools=['shell'] listeners=['tool/call'] -> deepseek-v4.1-flash
model swapped:     services=['llm'] tools=['shell'] listeners=['tool/call'] -> gpt-6-astra
shell unloaded:    services=['llm'] tools=[] listeners=[]

session log: 8 events -> 4 model-visible messages
   user       Investigate the failing service
   assistant  Checking pods. [shell: kubectl get pods]
   tool       api-7f 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff
   assistant  The api pod is crash-looping; reading its logs next.

fork at event 5: 6 events; last derived message -> ('user', 'Actually, check the database first')
replaying the same log always yields the same messages: True

Swapping the model adapter leaves every other plugin untouched, and unloading the shell plugin removes both its tool and its audit listener — nothing leaks. The session half shows why dsh can resume, fork and replay: the model's messages are a pure function of the log.

06 Turns, Steps and Events: the Agent Loop

In dsh a step is one model request plus the tools it calls; a turn is zero or more steps — it opens before its first input is claimed and closes once nothing is owed. The default driver is the core/agent-loop plugin. Watch a turn emit its events:

▶ One turn, two steps Event names from the architecture document; payloads illustrative.
Durable session events (turn/*, step/*, system/message, user/message, assistant/message, tool/*) are written to the log; live events such as agent/pre-step, agent/request and agent/assistant-stream are extension points plugins can hook.

07 Durable, Event-Sourced Sessions

The session log is append-only and is the source of truth for all agent state; session history — including the messages sent to the model — is derived from it, not stored separately. Its guiding invariant is "model-visible means logged": a runtime check verifies that every model request can be reconstructed from the log. Failed, retried and cancelled attempts are kept too (assistant/attempt). Logs are JSONL files (session.vN.jsonl, optionally zstd-compressed) behind a pluggable SessionPersistence interface.

▶ Log → projection, replay and fork Click an event to fork there.

08 Capability Seams

Each swappable capability is a seam with three roles: a service definition (the interface), one or more service providers (implementations) and consumers. Pick a seam and swap its provider — the consumers never change:

09 The Tool Runtime

Tools are plugins that register typed definitions with ctx.tools. Each call passes through validation, permission and policy checks, runs under an execution mode with timeouts, and returns a result that the loop can use — failures included. Pick a call:

▶ Through the tool runtime Simplified pipeline; policies are configurable per tool and agent.
📐 Typed definitions & validationSchema-based tool definitions; calls validated before execution.
🔐 Permissions & policyAllow / deny / ask per tool and agent; sandbox and approval policy ship in dsh-base.
⚡ Execution & parallel safetyCalls run through execution-service plugins (shell, filesystem, subprocess); independent, safe calls can run in parallel.
⏱️ Cooperative timeoutsPrevent hanging tools; failures return as results so the loop continues.

10 MCP Architecture (Optional)

dsh can connect to external MCP servers, whose tools are registered in the same tool runtime under server-qualified names such as mcp__github__create_issue. But no MCP server is enabled by default: the MCP client ships as a dependency, and you enable servers deliberately — because each server command is trusted executable code that runs outside the agent sandbox.

▶ Enable a server Toggle servers; watch tools appear in the registry.

11 SDK and Automation Entrypoints

The sdk profile serves SDK clients over newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdio until shutdown or disconnect; clients exist for TypeScript and Python (deepseek-harness-sdk on PyPI) and any language that speaks JSON-RPC. The acp profile runs an automation-only Agent Client Protocol server that reserves stdout for ACP frames.

▶ JSON-RPC frames over stdio Illustrative method names; press play.
Developer-preview caveat: a public repository discussion (#1238) notes that there is not yet a session/cancel request on the SDK wire — killing the runtime process is currently the way to abandon a turn.

Key takeaway: dsh is an open, self-hosted, plugin-composed agent runtime. Its differentiator is the replaceable plugin seams — model, tools, session, storage, loop and more — around an explicit event-sourced session spine. That buys maximum flexibility and composability, at the cost of higher engineering and operational ownership, in a developer preview whose APIs will change.
The product in one paragraph
Where OpenAI and Anthropic sell the harness as a service, DeepSeek open-sourced one and made it maximally decomposable. On the Cordis framework, every capability — model adapter, tool, session store, sandbox, loop, UI — is a plugin with reversible effects, composed into profiles (web, headless, sdk, sdk-minimal, acp) from bundles over a shared dsh-base. An append-only JSONL session log is the single source of truth, from which everything the model sees is derived and checked. Security defaults are conservative — no MCP servers until you enable them, sandbox and approval policy in the base bundle — but the operational burden is yours. It is the clearest reference implementation of the harness ideas in this series, and, as a developer preview, not yet a stable platform.

⚠️ Notes

The source infographic matches the repository well; corrections and refinements: (1) its example session log uses dotted event names (session.start, model.response.delta, tool.result); dsh's documented durable events use slash names — turn/start, step/start, user/message, assistant/message, tool/call, turn/end — and files are named session.vN.jsonl (optionally zstd); (2) profiles — it treats sdk-minimal like the others, but it is the one profile that does not stack dsh-base; (3) MCP — "no MCP server enabled by default" is correct, and the reason matters: server commands are trusted code running outside the agent sandbox; (4) the package families panel is a reasonable summary of the repository's layout, but individual package names change quickly in the preview — rely on the repository. Launch-star figures are one tracker's reported counts; interactive diagrams are simplified and the Python miniature is a teaching model.
